## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Survey what is actually working, right now, to attract interested learners to sign up for email mailing lists / newsletters, and diagnose why some approaches succeed while others fail.

CONTEXT ABOUT THE REQUESTER (for the niche-transfer filter, not the main scope):
- Mark runs Agile Pain Relief, a solo/small B2B consultancy teaching Scrum, Kanban, and Agile methods, now pivoting toward helping knowledge workers thrive with Generative AI.
- Audience = working professionals (Scrum Masters, product people, engineering leaders, knowledge workers).
- His current list-building tactics are NOT working: (a) a downloadable lead magnet, and (b) a quiz on Generative AI failure modes. Part of the value here is understanding WHY these two specific approaches may be underperforming.

SCOPE = "broad + niche filter": Survey what's working across creators, newsletter operators, course-sellers, coaches, consultants, and professional educators generally. Then explicitly flag which tactics transfer to a solo B2B expert selling training/thought leadership in the Agile + GenAI space, and why.

EVIDENCE BAR (report must include a mix of all four):
1. Named examples + numbers: specific people/companies with conversion rates, list-growth figures, or before/after data, cited to a source.
2. Practitioner case studies: detailed write-ups of what someone tried and why it worked or failed.
3. Benchmark / industry data: aggregate opt-in rates by lead-magnet type, channel, quiz vs ebook vs newsletter, average landing-page conversion rates, etc.
4. Mechanism explanations: the behavioral/psychological "why it works" behind each tactic.

CHANNELS = no preference: cover all major acquisition surfaces (website/blog on-site opt-ins, content upgrades, exit intent, quizzes; LinkedIn and other social; YouTube/video; podcasts; SEO; paid; referral/viral; partnerships/newsletter cross-promotion/recommendations like beehiiv/Substack) and let the evidence show where the leverage is.

SPECIFIC QUESTIONS THE REPORT SHOULD ANSWER:
- What lead-magnet / opt-in formats convert best today, and what are typical opt-in conversion rates by format (ebook/PDF vs quiz vs mini-course vs template/toolkit vs free email course vs live event/webinar vs community)? Cite benchmark data.
- Why do generic downloadable PDFs and quizzes often underperform now? What makes a quiz work vs fail specifically?
- What is working best for B2B / professional-services / expert-led audiences specifically (vs consumer creators)?
- Evidence on newsletter-first / "the newsletter IS the product" growth (Substack/beehiiv/ConvertKit era), recommendation networks, and cross-promotion.
- The role of the offer/promise and positioning vs the format: does specificity of promise beat format choice?
- Concrete before/after examples where someone changed their opt-in and measurably improved sign-ups.
- 3-5 concrete, prioritized recommendations for what Mark specifically should test next, grounded in the evidence.

Prioritize recent evidence (roughly 2022-2026) since tactics have shifted with AI and platform changes. Cite every claim.

3 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize into a polished, well-organized Markdown report.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] By lead-magnet format, giveaways/contests convert highest (29.37%), followed by learning resources (27.4%), interactive tools (26.44%), and reports/eBooks (24.61%); discounts convert lowest at 16.2% and plain newsletters/updates at 17.46%.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.mailerlite.com/blog/best-lead-magnet-statistics (primary)
Quote: "Giveaways/Contests 29.37% | Learning Resources 27.4% | Interactive Tools 26.44% | Reports/eBooks 24.61% ... Newsletters/Updates 17.46% | Discounts 16.2%"
Verifier evidence (high): All six numbers in the claim match the primary MailerLite source exactly (verified via WebFetch of https://www.mailerlite.com/blog/best-lead-magnet-statistics): Giveaways/Contests 29.37%, Learning Resources 27.4%, Interactive Tools 26.44%, Reports/eBooks 24.61%, Newsletters/Updates 17.46% (2nd-lowest), Discounts 16.2% (lowest). Ordering is accurate. Data is first-party, large-sample (41,000+ forms, 10,000+ paid users each with ≥100 conversions), and current (published March 13, 2026). Independent WebSearch corroborates the pattern (Formstack's 650,000-form study also found contests convert highest). Only caveat: 'conversion rate' = form-submit-after-open, not landing-page/list-growth rate — but the claim faithfully reports what the source measured and does not overreach.

### [1] Direct recommendations from current subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral) is ranked the single most effective newsletter growth strategy, cited by 42% of newsletter professionals, with partner/co-marketing cross-promotion ranking second.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/state-of-newsletters (primary)
Quote: "42% rank direct recommendations from current subscribers as the most effective growth strategy"
Verifier evidence (high): Both components of the claim are directly confirmed by the primary source, HubSpot's 2025 State of Newsletters Report (survey of 400+ newsletter professionals). The report states verbatim: "42% rank direct recommendations, via word of mouth or online, from current subscribers as the most effective strategy, followed by brands or co-marketing partners sharing the newsletter on their own channels." This matches the claim exactly on (a) the 42% figure, (b) direct recommendations/word-of-mouth being the single top-ranked growth strategy, and (c) partner/co-marketing cross-promotion ranking second. Independent secondary coverage (Selling Signals, ChartLocal, RADAAR) corroborates the same 42% figure and framing. The source is recent (2025), current for a fast-moving field, and is a methodologically-based practitioner survey rather than a press-release cherry-pick. Caveat: the report gives only the #1 and #2 rankings, not a full ordered list with percentages for lower ranks, but the claim does not overreach beyond what is stated.

### [2] There is a large gap between typical and top-performing B2B newsletters: per Mailchimp data, the median typical B2B organization adds 1 new subscriber per month while the top quartile median adds 69 per month.
Vote: 1-1 · Source: https://databox.com/grow-newsletter-subscribers-b2b (secondary)
Quote: "Median new subscribers for typical B2B organizations: 1 per month ... Top quartile median: 69 new subscribers per month"
Verifier evidence (low): The Databox article (databox.com/grow-newsletter-subscribers-b2b, May 2023) confirms the exact figures: median new subscribers for B2B = "one" per month (n=83 contributors), top quartile median = "69 new subscribers within the same period." The claim transcribes both numbers accurately and is not contradicted, not outdated (2023, within scope), and not marketing fluff. TWO CAVEATS that weaken (not refute) it: (1) Attribution — the claim says "per Mailchimp data," but this is NOT an official Mailchimp published benchmark; it is Databox's own "Mailchimp Benchmarks for B2B Companies" benchmark GROUP (companies that connected Mailchimp accounts to Databox's analytics tool). Databox is the actual source. (2) Methodology — "1 per month" is a fragile, noisy single-month snapshot from a small, self-selected pool (83 contributors), not a robust longitudinal benchmark. The core numeric claim is faithfully cited, so it survives, but it should be presented as a Databox benchmark-group figure with the small-sample caveat, not as authoritative "Mailchimp data."


## Refuted claims (for transparency)
- "Across 41,000+ forms and pop-ups from 10,000+ paid MailerLite users, the average opt-in conversion rate is 22.16%, establishing a current benchmark for email sign-up forms." (https://www.mailerlite.com/blog/best-lead-magnet-statistics, vote 0-3)
- "Learning resources are recommended as the optimal lead magnet for most businesses (over higher-converting giveaways) because they deliver high value and solve an immediate problem for the person who signs up." (https://www.mailerlite.com/blog/best-lead-magnet-statistics, vote 0-2)
- "Interactive quizzes convert far higher than static landing pages: 40.1% start-to-lead for engaged quiz users vs a 6.6% median landing page conversion rate across 41K pages, indicating format alone can create large opt-in differences." (https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/lead-magnet-conversion-benchmarks-2026-b2b-data-reference, vote 0-3)
## Unverified claims (19 — verifier agents failed; neither confirmed nor refuted)
- "Data-and-research-backed content is the single strongest driver of B2B buyer action, with 51% of B2B buyers naming it the #1 reason they agree to a sales call, ahead of shareable stats or thought leadership." (https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/lead-magnet-conversion-benchmarks-2026-b2b-data-reference, 2/3 votes errored)
- "Among B2B newsletter operators surveyed, landing pages are the most-cited subscriber collection method (35%+), ahead of subscription bars (just under 20%)." (https://databox.com/grow-newsletter-subscribers-b2b, 2/3 votes errored)
- "Interact quizzes convert visitors to leads at an average 40.1% start-to-lead rate, a figure that has stayed roughly flat since 2013 across 80M+ generated leads." (https://www.tryinteract.com/blog/quiz-conversion-rate-report/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Quizzes in the coaching/courses category convert at 44.9% start-to-lead, higher than e-commerce (37.6%) and service providers (42.2%)." (https://www.tryinteract.com/blog/quiz-conversion-rate-report/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "The mechanism behind high-converting quizzes in 2026 is that they act as 'personalized question answering lead magnets' answering questions people want answered about themselves." (https://www.tryinteract.com/blog/quiz-conversion-rate-report/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Interactive quizzes report a 40.1-47.3% start-to-lead rate while ebooks/whitepapers convert at only 4-8% at the landing-page level, but the quiz figure counts only already-engaged users, not total visitors, so the two numbers are not directly comparable." (https://subpage.co/lead-magnet-conversion-benchmarks-2026/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Checklists/cheatsheets convert at 24-42% and free tools/calculators at 28-42% opt-in, outperforming ebooks/whitepapers (4-8%)." (https://subpage.co/lead-magnet-conversion-benchmarks-2026/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Quiz funnels convert 30-50% of visitors who start into email subscribers, versus a 3-10% opt-in rate for standard PDF lead-magnet links." (https://www.kyleads.com/blog/quiz-funnels-vs-lead-magnets/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Static PDF lead magnets underperform because they do not adapt to individual needs and attract free-content seekers without purchase intent, producing lower lead quality than quizzes." (https://www.kyleads.com/blog/quiz-funnels-vs-lead-magnets/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Interactive quizzes convert far better than static formats, with AI-adaptive quizzes averaging a 47.3% opt-in conversion rate (up to 63.8% in beauty/wellness), per a ScoreApp analysis of 22,000 quiz funnels." (https://www.amraandelma.com/lead-magnet-conversion-statistics/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Average landing page conversion is reported at 23.4%, with AI-personalized pages at 37.1% versus static pages at 19.2%, attributed to a HubSpot analysis of 150,000+ landing pages." (https://www.amraandelma.com/lead-magnet-conversion-statistics/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Average email opt-in conversion rate is about 1.95%, with the bottom 25% of marketers at 0.8% and top performers reaching 6.5% (per Sumo data cited by Encharge)." (https://encharge.io/lead-magnet-examples/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Adding a content upgrade to a blog post raised the opt-in rate from 0.37% to 4.14%, a 1000%+ improvement (Sleeknote case study)." (https://encharge.io/lead-magnet-examples/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Wandering Aimfully's entrepreneur quiz converted at 38.8% and generated nearly $300,000 in revenue plus a 400% increase in email subscribers with no change in website traffic." (https://encharge.io/lead-magnet-examples/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Interactive quiz funnels convert at ~40% on average, versus 3-10% for static PDF/checklist lead magnets, per this vendor's framing." (https://getaiform.com/blog/quiz-funnels-vs-static-lead-magnets-interactive-content-conversion-2026, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Interactive content converts roughly 70% of the time vs 36% for passive content, attributed to DemandGen Report." (https://getaiform.com/blog/quiz-funnels-vs-static-lead-magnets-interactive-content-conversion-2026, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Quiz funnels fail primarily due to a weak landing page: a poor landing page produces a poor conversion rate because visitors never reach the quiz itself." (https://www.scoreapp.com/quiz-funnel-mistakes/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "Clear, benefit-plain quiz copy converts better than clever/creative copy (e.g. 'How Eco Friendly are you?' beats 'Eco Warriors Unite')." (https://www.scoreapp.com/quiz-funnel-mistakes/, 3/3 votes errored)
- "PDF lead-magnet landing pages convert at 1-5% opt-in, while quiz funnels achieve 30-50% completion rates, making quizzes far higher-converting than static PDFs." (https://brothersautomate.com/blog/quiz-funnels-vs-pdf-lead-magnets/, 3/3 votes errored)

Mention in caveats that 19 claim(s) could not be verified due to infrastructure errors.

## Instructions
Write a complete research report in GitHub-flavored Markdown. Structure:
1. **Executive summary** — 4-6 sentences directly answering the research question.
2. **Findings** — group the confirmed claims into coherent themed sections with `##` headings. Merge semantic duplicates and combine their sources. Under each finding, cite the source URL(s) inline as Markdown links and note confidence (high/medium/low) based on source quality and vote margin. Include the concrete numbers/benchmarks from the claims.
3. **What this means for a solo B2B expert (Agile + GenAI)** — a niche-transfer section flagging which tactics apply to Mark and why.
4. **Recommendations** — 3-5 concrete, prioritized things to test next.
5. **Caveats** — what's uncertain, weak sources, time-sensitivity.
6. **Open questions** — 2-4 that emerged but weren't answered.

Cite every claim with its source link. Output ONLY the Markdown report, no preamble.

- copilot-read-pdf: Extract the full text of a PDF as Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user wants to read, summarize, or quote a PDF file (in the vault or an absolute path). Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-web-fetch: Fetch and read the full contents of a specific web page (URL) as clean Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a link or asks you to open, read, or summarize a particular page — not for an open-ended web search. Requires an active Copilot Plus license; without it, use your own fetch tool instead.

Use when the user asks to search online, look something up on the internet, or needs up-to-date facts beyond the vault. Prefer reading the vault for anything about the user's own notes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-youtube-transcript: Fetch the transcript of a YouTube video using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a YouTube URL and wants its contents, a summary, or quotes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.

Needs the Miyo desktop app installed and running.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
